issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the petitioner under Section 376 AB of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) should be set aside.

facts: The petitioner was convicted by a Trial Court for kidnapping and raping a 7-year-old girl.
The Trial Court found that the prosecution had presented "damning evidence" to establish guilt, including witness testimonies and corroborating medical evidence.
The conviction was under several sections, including Section 376 AB of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The High Court had previously commuted the petitioner's initial death sentence to life imprisonment but upheld the conviction.
The petitioner appealed to the Supreme Court, seeking to have the conviction under Section 376 AB IPC set aside.
law: Section 376 AB of the IPC prescribes punishment for the rape of a child under 12 years of age.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence on record and agreed with the lower courts' findings.
The Court noted that the guilt of the petitioner under Section 376 AB IPC had been "conclusively proved" by the prosecution.
The evidence included oral testimonies from witnesses who found the convict violating the victim and medical evidence that unerringly pointed to his guilt.
The Court's primary focus was on the appropriateness of the sentence, not the validity of the conviction itself, as the evidence of guilt was considered overwhelming.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's plea to set aside the conviction. It explicitly stated it was "maintaining the conviction of the petitioner-convict under Section 376 AB, IPC" because his guilt had been conclusively proven by the evidence presented at trial.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed on the petitioner for the offence under Section 376 AB of the IPC requires modification.

facts: The petitioner was convicted under Section 376 AB of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for raping a seven-year-old girl.
The Trial Court initially sentenced him to capital punishment.
On appeal, the High Court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, which under Section 376 AB means imprisonment for the remainder of the convict's natural life.

The petitioner appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing for a further reduction of the sentence, citing his age (40 at the time of the offense), lack of criminal history, and the possibility of rehabilitation.
law: Section 376 AB of the IPC provides for two alternative punishments for the offense: (1) the death penalty, or (2) rigorous imprisonment for a term of not less than 20 years, which may extend to life imprisonment (meaning for the convict's natural life).
The provision also mandates the imposition of a fine that is just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim.
The Supreme Court has the power to impose a modified, fixed-term sentence that is greater than the minimum prescribed term but less than imprisonment for the convict's entire natural life.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged the need for a deterrent punishment for the severe nature of the crime.

However, it also considered mitigating factors, including the petitioner's age, the period of incarceration he had already served, and the High Court's own observation that the possibility of his reformation could not be ruled out.
The Court balanced these aggravating and mitigating factors and determined that neither the minimum sentence of 20 years nor the maximum of imprisonment for natural life was appropriate.
It decided that a fixed-term sentence would be just in this case.
The Court also noted that the High Court had overlooked the mandatory requirement to impose a fine for the victim's rehabilitation and rectified this omission.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal and modified the sentence. It commuted the sentence of life imprisonment (for the remainder of the petitioner's natural life) to a fixed term of 30 years of rigorous imprisonment. Additionally, it imposed a fine of Rupees One Lakh to be paid to the victim for her medical expenses and rehabilitation.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that while the crime was committed in an extremely depraved and barbaric manner, the sentence should be modified because there were significant mitigating factors. Specifically, the prosecution failed to show any criminal antecedents of the accused, and the possibility of his rehabilitation and reformation had not been ruled out. Therefore, the court determined that an alternative punishment to the maximum sentence would be sufficient to meet the ends of justice.
legal_tests_applied: A balancing test weighing the aggravating circumstances of the crime (extreme depravity and barbaric manner) against the mitigating circumstances of the offender (no criminal history, possibility of rehabilitation and reformation).

Application of the statutory mandate under Section 376 AB, IPC, which requires the imposition of a fine that is just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim, in addition to the term of imprisonment.
why_appellant_lost: The court did not provide any reasoning for upholding the conviction, indicating that no grounds were found to set it aside. The entire analysis focused on the appropriateness of the sentence.

The sentence was not reduced further due to the court's acknowledgment of the "extreme depravity and the barbaric manner in which the crime was committed," which justified a severe, long-term sentence.
why_respondent_won: The conviction was maintained as the court found no basis to interfere with the trial court's and High Court's findings on the petitioner's guilt.
The court imposed a substantial sentence of 30 years of rigorous imprisonment without the possibility of early release, affirming the gravity of the offence.
The court corrected an error by the High Court and imposed a fine of Rupees One Lakh, as mandated by Section 376 AB, IPC, to be paid to the victim for medical expenses and rehabilitation.
policy_considerations: The court considered the penological principles of reformation and rehabilitation, noting that the "possibility of being rehabilitation and reformation has abo not been ruled out" and that there was nothing on record "to suggest that he cannot be useful for the society."
The court enforced the legislative policy embedded in Section 376 AB, IPC, that sentencing must include a financial component for the direct benefit and rehabilitation of the victim.
